title: Isfahan, c. 1408-9: the governor's summons
dramatic_question: The governor of Fars sends for you. Do you go?

invariants.text: Back in Isfahan you took up teaching, meaning to live quietly in contemplation (gūsha-nishīnī), until Pīr-Muḥammad, Temür's grandson and governor of Fars, summoned you to Shiraz.
invariants.detail: The governor's full name is Pīr-Muḥammad b. ʿUmar-Shaykh. Melvin-Koushki cites no source for this passage and marks its dates 'c.'.

invariants.text: Pīr-Muḥammad was murdered in 812/1409 and his brother Iskandar Mīrzā took his place in Shiraz. Nothing you do prevents it.
None of the letters Melvin-Koushki lists is addressed to Pīr-Muḥammad, and nothing on those pages shows what you offered him or what he gave you.

prose: You are back in Isfahan and you have taken up teaching. You mean to live the way the sources call gūsha-nishīnī, the life of contemplation in a corner. It does not last.

Pīr-Muḥammad b. ʿUmar-Shaykh, a grandson of Temür, governs Fars from Shiraz, and he sends for you. Melvin-Koushki tells this without naming a source and dates it only 'c. 1408-9', so what you have is his summary of the episode, not a document from it.
The record does not say what the governor offered. What you can weigh is the quiet you meant to keep against a summons from the man who rules your province.

choices.label: Answer the summons: go to Shiraz and take a place at Pīr-Muḥammad's court.
choices.feedback: Melvin-Koushki reports that you went and were made a member of his court. He gives no source and marks the dates 'c.', so treat the detail as his summary. What is missing matters: no letter to Pīr-Muḥammad is in the list, so the record cannot tell you what you asked or received. His murder in 812/1409 is the fixed point that ends this tie; the next scene shows what you stood on afterwards.

choices.label: Refuse the summons: stay in Isfahan, keep teaching, and keep out of the court.
choices.feedback: No source has you refusing. Melvin-Koushki has you summoned and made a member of the court, and the honours that follow presuppose it. The quiet life is what Melvin-Koushki says you kept trying to return to, not something the sources show you keeping. The game returns you to the record: you go, and the murder of 1409 arrives regardless. What you gained and paid here stays in your ledger; the story then rejoins the record.
costs: You keep your students and stay clear of the court, so exposure falls. You forgo the governor's stipend, and your household is poorer.
